Twenty years later, her shaved head wrapped in a scarf, Su Lina left the little room where they lived, alone, deep in the night. Two days later a bloated, bald-headed woman's body was fished out of Suzhou Creek, yet Zhongliang betrayed no excess of grief. He only sat up the whole night at the head of the bed and smoked, and found himself thinking, unbidden, of Zhou San, who had likewise died in Suzhou Creek; thinking of Xiufen, his first woman; of his father, Xu Delin; of his mother and the old bamboo-worker; and of Mr. Pan, and of Father Brown. In that one night Zhongliang called to mind all the dead who had ever touched his life.

Another ten years passed, and Zhongliang retired in due form from the Jing'an District Post and Telecommunications Bureau. He took Su Lina's ashes and left Shanghai, going back to Xietang, his mother's home town, and buried his wife by that river. Every year when Qingming came, he would write his love a long letter in a tiny, fly's-head regular hand, and then burn it before her grave. And in the firelight he watched, again and again, Su Lina standing there before him, the look on her face languid and indifferent.
